episodes.caption: Some people run on discipline. Some on purpose. Some on avoidance. All three look the same from the outside. What's yours?

episodes.title: The Night Shift

slides.text:
Episode 24

THE NIGHT SHIFT

Reshma.

The nurse who taught me where the good chai was on my first week. Who covered for me when I cried in the supply room after losing my first patient. Who hums 'Pal Pal Dil Ke Paas' during night rounds and makes the whole ward feel less like a hospital.

She was on the floor of the nurses' station when I got there.

Conscious. Breathing. But her face was grey.

'Reshma—'

'I'm fine. I just got dizzy. Too many doubles.'

She wasn't fine. The ECG said what she wouldn't.

Cardiac arrhythmia. Supraventricular tachycardia.

Her heart had been beating wrong for months. Maybe longer.

'The palpitations you mentioned to Dr. Rao in January?' the cardiologist said.

'I thought it was just stress.'

'It wasn't.'

Reshma — who checks on every patient, every drip, every monitor — hadn't checked on herself.

The irony wasn't lost on anyone.

Least of all me.

Because I do the same thing. Every single day.

I sat with her that night. Not as coordinator. As me.

'You're hovering,' she said.

'I'm sitting.'

'You're hovering while sitting. It's a skill.'

Even from the bed, she was the funny one.

'Reshma. Why didn't you get the ECG?'

She looked at the ceiling.

'Same reason you don't call your mother back.'

I went still.

'We both know what the test will show. So we don't take it.'

She said it gently. The way she says everything. But it landed like a brick.

Day two. She was stable. Medication adjusting the rhythm.

Her mother came from Nagpur. Small woman. Enormous worry.

Reshma introduced me: 'Maa, this is my favourite person in the hospital.'

'You're in the hospital,' her mother said flatly. 'There is no favourite anything.'

Mothers.

I helped Reshma's mother navigate the food options, the visiting hours, the medical terms.

The same things I do for strangers every day.

But this time my hands were shaking.

That evening, Reshma was asleep. The medication made her drowsy.

I sat in the chair and looked at her.

The Kishore Kumar humming was quiet.

And I thought — for the first time clearly —

I have been watching people's reckonings for twenty-three weeks.

The founder who learned he wasn't irreplaceable.
The old man who learned to braid.
The doctor who learned what fifteen percent feels like.
The single mother whose seven-year-old drew the truth.

Every single one of them faced their thing.

And I've been writing about mine in a Notes app.

Five sentences. Locked. Unsent.

Watching. Always watching.

When is it my turn?

Reshma woke up at midnight. Saw me still there.

'Go home.'

'No.'

'You're not my coordinator.'

'I'm not here as your coordinator.'

She reached for my hand.

'I'm going to be fine. The arrhythmia is manageable. Medication. Follow-ups.'

'I know.'

'Then why are you crying?'

I didn't have an answer. Or I had too many.

Because you're my person here. Because if you're in the bed, who do I sit with at 2 AM? Because you're the only one in Mumbai who knows about Indore. Because I can't lose anyone else to a heart that wasn't watched carefully enough.

I said none of it.

She heard all of it.

I walked home at 1 AM. The streets were empty. Mumbai at its quietest.

I took out my phone.

Opened the Notes app.

Five sentences. All about Indore. All true. All locked.

I read them. From the beginning.

1. I left Indore because I couldn't watch Papa die.
2. I was pre-med. I understood every word on his chart. I left anyway.
3. I left because nobody was seeing me either.
4. When knowing isn't enough, you have to choose — stay and feel it, or leave and carry it.
5. I left her to carry the house alone.

Five sentences. One story.

My story.

I added a sixth:

I chose patient care because I couldn't give it to the one patient who mattered.

Then I did something I hadn't done in eleven months.

I pressed share.

Not to Maa. Not yet.

To Reshma.

Seen. 1:14 AM.

No reply.

Just a heart emoji.

That was enough.

Reshma was discharged on day four. Medication. Follow-ups. No more double shifts.

She came back to work a week later. Light duties.

The first thing she did was hum. Kishore Kumar. 'Pal Pal Dil Ke Paas.'

The ward exhaled.

She found me at the canteen. 2 AM chai. Our usual.

'I read your six sentences,' she said. 'Every day since you sent them.'

'And?'

'And you need to call your mother.'

I nodded.

'I know.'

'Not 'I know.' Actually call her.'

She pushed my phone toward me.

'Not today. But soon. Before it's too late for one of you.'

She wasn't talking about death.

She was talking about the distance becoming permanent.

The kind no train can close.

I picked up the phone.

Not to call. Not yet.

But I moved it to my right hand.

Closer.

episodes.synopsis: Reshma — the night shift nurse who hums Kishore Kumar, who has been a background presence since episode one — collapses during a shift. What they thought was exhaustion turns out to be something else: a cardiac arrhythmia that's been hiding behind double shifts and ignored palpitations. She's admitted to the same ward she works on. For the first time, the coordinator isn't meeting a patient — she's sitting beside a friend. The professional distance she's maintained for twenty-three episodes dissolves completely. And in that collapse, she faces the truth she's been circling: you can't keep caring for everyone else's reckoning while avoiding your own.
episodes.caption: We take care of everyone except the one person who takes care of us. Who's your person — and when did you last check on them?

episodes.title: The Quiet Hours

slides.text:
Episode 25

THE QUIET HOURS

I woke up without an alarm for the first time in months.

7:12 AM. Light through the curtain. The sound of the building's water pump. A crow arguing with another crow.

I made chai. Not hospital chai — the kind Maa makes. Elaichi. Too much sugar. Boiled till the colour is almost orange.

I stood at the window and drank it.

Mumbai was doing what Mumbai does. Moving. Everyone going somewhere.

Today, I'm not going anywhere.

Today, I'm staying.

I went for a walk. No destination.

Past the auto stand where I take the 7 AM to work. The driver waved — he didn't recognise me in regular clothes.

Past the chai stall. Past the pharmacy. Past the building where I once saw a man carrying a harmonium into a hospital.

Mumbai is louder when you're not rushing through it.

I noticed things I'd missed.

A father braiding his daughter's hair at a bus stop.

A woman with a timetable pinned inside her tiffin bag.

A boy bowling an imaginary ball at a lamp post.

A nurse in scrubs, heading to a shift, humming something.

Twenty-four patients. And the city was full of them.

I walked to Marine Drive.

Sat on the parapet. Face to the sea.

And I took out my phone.

Not the Notes app. Not this time.

The call log.

Maa — missed call. April 2.
Maa — missed call. March 28.
Maa — missed call. March 19.
Maa — answered. 47 seconds. March 3.

Forty-seven seconds. That was our last real call. Forty-seven seconds of 'haan maa, theek hoon, busy hoon, baad mein call karti hoon.'

Yes maa, I'm fine, I'm busy, I'll call later.

Later.

Always later.

The sea didn't care about later. It just kept coming.

I sat there for twenty minutes.

The sea came in. Went out. Came in.

I thought about the six sentences.

1. I left Indore because I couldn't watch Papa die.
2. I was pre-med. I understood every word on his chart. I left anyway.
3. I left because nobody was seeing me either.
4. When knowing isn't enough, you have to choose — stay and feel it, or leave and carry it.
5. I left her to carry the house alone.
6. I chose patient care because I couldn't give it to the one patient who mattered.

Six sentences. The truest thing I've ever written.

But sentences aren't enough.

At some point, you have to use your voice.

I pressed call.

Three rings.

'Beta?'

Her voice. The same voice. Unchanged by eleven months of distance.

'Maa.'

'Tu theek hai?' Are you okay?

The same question from episode fourteen. From every missed call. The question she always leads with because she's afraid I'll hang up if she starts with anything else.

'Maa... nahi. Theek nahi hoon.'

No. I'm not okay.

Silence.

Not the bad kind. The kind that means she's sitting down. The kind that means she has time. The kind that means — finally — I can talk.

So I did.

I don't know how long we talked.

I told her about the hospital. About the patients. About the startup founder and the braid and the cricket boy and the journalist.

I told her about Reshma and the 2 AM chai.

I told her about the Notes app.

And then I told her the thing.

'I left because I couldn't watch Papa go. And I'm sorry. Not for leaving. For pretending I left for any other reason.'

Maa was quiet for a long time.

Then:

'Beta, I knew.'

'You knew?'

'A mother knows. I knew the day you packed. You packed his photo last. Wrapped it in your dupatta. A girl running toward something doesn't wrap her father's photo like that.'

She knew.

All this time.

She knew and she let me go anyway.

Because that's what mothers do.

They let you go and carry the house alone and answer every call you don't make.

We talked for forty-seven minutes.

Forty-seven. Not seconds. Minutes.

She told me about the house. The neighbours. The mango tree that finally fruited after six years.

She told me about Papa's last month. The things I missed. The things she carried.

She didn't make me feel guilty. She just told me. Like she'd been waiting for someone to tell.

'Maa, I want to come home.'

'Then come.'

'Not forever. But for a weekend. Soon.'

'The mangoes are ready. Come before they fall.'

Mangoes.

Come before they fall.

That's how my mother says 'I love you and I've been waiting and please don't take another eleven months.'

I laughed. She laughed.

The sound of two women on a phone, eleven months late, laughing about mangoes.

That's the sound of coming home.

I walked home.

Slow. No auto. No rush.

The phone was warm in my pocket. The call still open in my recent log.

47 minutes.

I passed the hospital. My hospital.

The night shift was ending. Day shift coming in.

Through the glass doors, I could see the corridor. The same corridor I walk every day.

But today I saw what I couldn't see from inside:

It's a good place.

Not because it heals people. Hospitals don't heal people. People heal people.

The old man with the rope braid. The physiotherapist who outranks a Colonel. The night nurse who hums Kishore Kumar.

I chose this work because of Papa.

But I'll stay because of them.

I got home. Made another chai. Maa's recipe.

Sat at the window.

Opened the Notes app.

Six sentences.

I read them one last time.

Then I deleted them.

Not because they weren't true.

Because I'd finally said them out loud.

The screen went blank.

And for the first time in eleven months, the quiet didn't feel like something I was hiding in.

It felt like something I was resting in.

The quiet hours.

Not the hospital's. Mine.

episodes.synopsis: No patient this time. This is her episode. A Saturday off — her first in weeks. The morning, the commute she doesn't have to make, the city she chose. She walks through Mumbai the way she's walked through twenty-four wards: observing, absorbing, carrying. Fragments from every patient surface. The startup founder's Slack. The old man's braid. Shastri sir's Sa. Reshma's heart emoji at 1:14 AM. And Indore. Always Indore. Today, she stops running. She calls her mother. Not to confess. Not to apologise. Just to talk. And in that conversation — imperfect, interrupted, full of long pauses — something loosens. The season ends the way it began: quietly. But she is not the same person who walked into this hospital eleven months ago.
